sections.section_summary:
The thirteen Science Working Group overviews summarise the science case of each SKAO community. Their requirements fall into a few recurring groups. Spectral-line work runs from the Galactic interstellar medium to cosmic dawn. Van Loon et al. treat masers, megamasers and recombination lines, Jing Wang et al. set out tiered HI galaxy surveys, Audard et al. cover the cycle of matter in the Milky Way, and Bianchi et al. cover astrochemistry and protoplanetary disks. These chapters depend on SKA-Mid Bands 2 and 5, on zoom-mode spectral resolution of 0.1-1 km/s, and on arcsecond-to-milliarcsecond beams. Continuum and polarimetric work (Hale et al., Vernstrom et al.) turns on survey speed and depth, which set how fast confusion-limited fields and dense rotation-measure grids can be built in Band 2 and with SKA-Low. Cosmology (Spinelli et al.) and Epoch of Reionisation science (Trott et al.) set out wide-area HI intensity mapping and 21-cm experiments of 1000 to 10,000 hours. The time-domain chapters form the remaining group: pulsars and pulsar timing arrays (Joshi et al., Bellomo et al.), transients (Miller-Jones et al.), solar and heliospheric physics (Zucca et al.) and cosmic-ray air showers (Huege et al.). These call on beamformed timing, fast imaging, millisecond cadence and commensal voltage buffering.

The observing modes the section relies on most are spectral-line and maser surveys, VLBI and astrometry, deep HI intensity mapping, pulsar timing arrays, and commensal or triggered transient observing. Several overviews give concrete survey setups. Vernstrom et al. tabulate the RM-grid densities reached at 0.5 and 2 uJy/beam in Band 2 and at 10 uJy/beam with SKA-Low, with integration times for AA* and AA4. Jing Wang et al. keep the 1,000-hour and 10,000-hour "wedding cake" HI tiers, now corrected for the measured RFI environment. Spinelli et al. assume a 5,000 deg2 Band 2 survey and a 20,000 deg2 Band 1 survey. Trott et al. restrict EoR work to 50-220 MHz and ask for short baselines with high surface-brightness sensitivity. Huege et al. show that SKA-Low can measure air showers at no cost to other programmes, as long as a particle-detector trigger can freeze the raw-voltage buffers in the tile processors. Zucca et al. set the solar requirements: snapshot dynamic range above 10^5, cadence of 50 ms or better, and data rates that can exceed 10 TB per hour.

The overviews differ sharply on AA* versus AA4. For EoR and Cosmic Dawn science, Trott et al. find that AA* and AA4 perform similarly. AA4 adds some core sensitivity and better surface-brightness sensitivity but does not change the uv-coverage in any qualitative way. Spinelli et al., in contrast, find that radio weak lensing and its cross-correlations cannot be done without AA4 baselines, while HI intensity mapping and continuum cosmology remain possible with AA*. Audard et al. report that twelve of thirteen Our Galaxy chapters ask for AA4. Bianchi et al. stress that protoplanetary-disk science needs the full AA4 SKA-Mid baselines. Van Loon et al. and Joshi et al. describe a gradient: AA* delivers first detections and roughly tenfold timing gains, and AA4 adds the sensitivity for tens-of-nanosecond timing and statistically complete samples. Bellomo et al. split their gravitational-wave targets between AA* and AA4 but urge that analysis begin during AA*. Several groups also ask for more than AA4. Van Loon et al. and Bianchi et al. both argue for a Band 6 receiver above 15 GHz, reaching up to about 24 GHz.

Nevertheless, the microphysics of matter above nuclear saturation density-and the transition between hadronic and exotic phases-remains uncertain.
The three-dimensional structure and global symmetry of the Milky Way's magnetic field remain incompletely characterized.
Solar energetic particle (SEP) events are a major space-weather hazard, yet the mechanisms by which particles are accelerated and released from the corona remain poorly understood.
Their origin is debated: competing models invoke magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) oscillations of flaring structures, periodic or bursty reconnection, and nonlinear wave-particle interactions.

However, such measurements are crucial to assess the importance of magnetic fields in the star formation process, as the few current observations suggest marginally supercritical conditions where the magnetic fields cannot prevent collapse but inhibit it, but it remains unclear if this is a biased result.

While several thousand have been detected to date (as either one-off events or repeating bursts), the nature of their progenitors remains unresolved, although the diversity of burst properties and host environments suggests that multiple progenitor channels may contribute (as discussed in the chapter by Curtin et al., 2026).
Large regions of this complex, multi-dimensional parameter space remain to be explored.

sections.section_summary:
The Sun, Earth and Planets section is dominated by solar and heliospheric physics, with a smaller group of papers on stars, exoplanets, the outer Solar System and terrestrial lightning. The solar chapters share a single observational premise. The radio Sun changes on sub-second and sub-MHz scales, and several bright and faint sources are often present on the disk at once, so the science depends on snapshot spectropolarimetric imaging with high dynamic range rather than on long synthesis integrations. Patra and Kansabanik want wideband, full-Stokes imaging to measure coronal and CME magnetic fields through free-free, gyroresonance and gyrosynchrotron emission and through Faraday rotation of background sources. Sharma, Kontar, Kumari, Morosan and Nakariakov focus on particle acceleration, radio-burst fine structure, solar energetic particles and quasi-periodic pulsations, and they ask for millisecond-to-sub-second cadence, kHz channels (including zoom and beamformed modes) and dense uv coverage. Mondal argues that SKA-Low sensitivity and a clean snapshot PSF are needed to characterise weak quiet-Sun transients carrying fluxes of tens of mSFU. Zhang, Raja and Chrysaphi turn propagation effects into diagnostics of coronal and solar-wind turbulence, using angular broadening of background sources along the solar track and the scattered images of solar bursts. Oberoi and Cheung set out the practical conditions that all of this depends on: attenuator characterisation, self-calibration in the strong-source regime, elastic correlator modes, triggered observing, and imaging tools that handle differential solar rotation and uniform weighting of the dense SKA-Mid core.

The observing modes are therefore almost entirely solar/heliospheric imaging, supplemented by tied-array and zoom configurations and by trigger-driven transient capture. For lightning, Hare requires raw-voltage buffer dumps rather than channelised data. The non-solar papers draw on other modes. Mohan and Vedantham use deep continuum and wide-field circular-polarisation surveys to reach active M dwarfs and star-planet interaction candidates; Vedantham proposes a southern-sky survey in 1 h pointings at 144 MHz with a Stokes V threshold near 140 microJy. Curiel relies on SKA-VLBI MultiView astrometry at 1-10 microarcsecond precision to find planets around ultracool dwarfs. Santos-Sanz needs deep Band 5b continuum integrations of about 5 h to detect thermal emission from trans-Neptunian objects at the 1.58 microJy (5 sigma) level.

The papers differ in what they expect from AA* compared with AA4. Several conclude that AA* already meets their core needs. Chrysaphi notes that the AA* frequency range covers every signal relevant to heliospheric turbulence and that a 6 km SKA-Low subarray already beats LOFAR in resolution. Hare expects AA* to give the baselines and sensitivity needed for new lightning science. For snapshot fidelity, however, the extra stations and intermediate baselines of AA4 matter. Cheung finds the AA* PSF less Gaussian for narrowband snapshots. Sharma points out that early SKA-Low assemblies lack the short baselines needed to image the extended disk. Mohan quotes 15.8 versus 10.2 microJy/beam in 1 h at 1.4 GHz for AA* and AA4. The most sensitivity-limited programmes depend on AA4: Santos-Sanz finds that AA* would detect only a few of the largest trans-Neptunian objects, Vedantham ties a substantial star-planet interaction yield to the roughly 10 microJy reach of SKA-Low AA4, and Curiel notes that AA* limits SKA-VLBI to one or perhaps four simultaneous beams.

sections.section_summary:
The Formation and Evolution of Stars section follows matter from cold prestellar cores through protostars, jets and planet-forming disks to evolved massive stars, supernova remnants and magnetars. Most of its science is built around SKA-Mid Band 5, and especially Band 5b (8.3-15.4 GHz). At these frequencies dust is optically thin, so the telescope can see into disk midplanes and dense envelopes that ALMA cannot reach. The astrochemistry chapters (Bianchi, Podio) target cyanopolyynes, carbon-chain radicals, benzonitrile and interstellar complex organic molecules with zoom-mode spectroscopy at 3-13 kHz resolution, with integrations of 10 to 1000 hours. The disk chapters (Garufi, Wu, Guidi) use Band 5b continuum to detect centimetre-sized pebbles and to resolve rings at about 0.05 arcsec, and they stack hydrogen recombination lines to separate photoevaporative from magnetised winds. Magnetic fields form a second strand. Bourke gives Zeeman forecasts for OH, CCS and C4H, and Loren-Anderson for carbon recombination lines. Bracco proposes synchrotron detection of starless cores with SKA-Low at 200 MHz and SKA-Mid Bands 1-2. Rygl uses maser surveys and time-domain maser monitoring.

The section relies mainly on four observing modes. The first is targeted spectral-line and maser observation, often with several zoom windows per band. The second is wide-field continuum surveying: Traficante's 630 deg2 Galactic-plane survey in Band 5b at 20 microJy/beam takes about 600 h, and Cavallaro's 70 percent sky survey in Band 2 targets ultracool dwarfs. The third is polarimetry, including Zeeman measurements, applied to jets, supernova remnants and dense cores. The fourth is SKA-VLBI astrometry, which Akahori uses for magnetar proper motions and parallaxes (50 microarcsec precision) and Ingallinera for OH masers in supernova remnants. Buemi, Ingallinera and Guidi all need matched beams in Band 2 and Band 5 to build spectral-index maps. Forbrich and Rygl add time-domain work coordinated with ALMA on accretion bursts and stellar flares. Several chapters (Sabatini, Forbrich, Bourke, Podio) press for a Band 6 receiver (15-50 GHz) to close the gap up to ALMA Band 1. Several chapters also count on the MeerKAT dishes receiving Band 5b receivers, which they estimate would raise line sensitivity by about 1.4 times.

The chapters agree broadly on what AA* and AA4 can each deliver. AA* already supports a substantial early programme. Bianchi finds that the lighter carbon chains in prestellar cores are detectable in 10 h at about 30 arcsec resolution. Rygl expects follow-up of maser flares and OH surveys of AGB stars once zoom mode is available. Bourke proposes AA* surveys of CCS and C4H to prepare for Zeeman work, and Sabatini reports most jet science as feasible from Science Verification onwards. Buemi's simulations show that AA* already partially resolves nebulae around Wolf-Rayet stars. In contrast, the demanding cases depend on the long baselines and full collecting area of AA4. Resolving the jet-launching region at about 4 au (Sabatini), resolving disk rings (Wu) and detecting faint disk lines on 100 au scales (Podio) all require AA4. Bracco finds that AA4 halves the time to detect a starless core with SKA-Low (below 50 h against below 100 h). The Galactic-plane survey grows from about 600 h at AA4 to about 1800 h at AA*, and its beam widens from 0.07 to 0.16 arcsec.

sections.section: From the Milky Way to Distant Galaxies
sections.section_summary:
The "From the Milky Way to Distant Galaxies" section covers three linked science drivers. The first is the magnetised, multiphase interstellar medium of the Milky Way. The second is the gas cycle and star formation in nearby galaxies. The third is the demography and physics of radio AGN, from parsec-scale jet bases to Mpc-scale lobes. On the Galactic side, Sun, Ma and Tahani set out Faraday rotation and Zeeman programmes to map magnetic fields in three dimensions. Sun02 and Miville-Deschenes use SKA-Low polarimetry and HI to map the Local Bubble, while XuYe and Imai rely on SKA-VLBI maser astrometry to map spiral structure and the nuclear stellar disk. Salas, Karska and Yamamoto place tight spectral demands on radio recombination lines, molecular absorption and cold neutral medium work, with channels as fine as 0.21 kHz and velocity resolution better than 0.5 km/s. For nearby galaxies, Rosolowsky, deBlok, Ramatsoku, Deg and HengxingPan set HI requirements in terms of column density and beam size. Typical targets are 1e19-1e20 cm^-2 at 10 arcsec in about 10 h, or 1 arcsec imaging that needs of order 100 h. The AGN papers rest mainly on Band 2 and Band 5 continuum surveys, which Prandoni and Kondapally frame as wide (about 1000 deg2 at 1 uJy/beam), deep (about 20-25 deg2 at 0.2 uJy/beam) and ultra-deep (1 deg2 at 0.05 uJy/beam) tiers. Other papers need milliarcsecond VLBI to isolate compact cores (Panessa, Baldi, DAmato).

The observing modes follow from these goals. Ultra-deep and wide-field continuum imaging dominate the extragalactic cases: star formation histories, faint AGN, dual AGN, JWST Little Red Dots and ultra-diffuse galaxies. Many of these papers ask for matched sub-arcsecond resolution from SKA-Low at 300 MHz up to Band 5b, so that spectra can be decomposed into thermal and non-thermal parts (Algera, Moldon, FangxiaAn, Tabatabaei). Polarimetry and RM-grid work is the next largest group. It ranges from an all-sky Band 2 RM grid at 2 arcsec (Sun01) to deep per-pointing Band 1 and Band 5 integrations of 20-450 h aimed at small-scale field structure (Ma). Spectral-line and maser modes cover water megamaser searches in Bands 5a/5b (Tarchi), CO J=1-0 at z of 7 or more in Band 5b (RanWang), and HI 21-cm absorption (Mahony). Several papers identify real gaps. Tarchi and Sawada-Satoh point out that nearby 22 GHz water masers fall above the 15.4 GHz ceiling. RanWang and Sawada-Satoh depend on a proposed Band 6 that is not part of the AA4 baseline, and Karska and Ma note that the Band 3 and 4 receivers are unfunded.

Several papers compare AA* with AA4 quantitatively. For low-surface-brightness HI, deBlok finds that the extra AA4 dishes add little column-density sensitivity, because they sit on long baselines, so AA* already meets 10 arcsec, 10 h HI goals. HengxingPan likewise finds the AA*-AA4 gap narrows at high resolution. In contrast, arcsecond HI imaging depends on AA4. Rosolowsky reports a noise level 13 times higher at AA* than at AA4 for a 1 arcsec beam, and Maccagni ties sub-kpc HI in nearby AGN to AA4. For continuum, Prandoni expects about four times coarser resolution and more confusion at AA*, with Band 2 times about twice and Band 5a times about three times those at AA4. Sun01 finds that AA4 halves the RM-grid integration per pointing, but notes that its funding and timeline are uncertain. Consequently, a subset of programmes is designed to run at AA*: Vidal on AME, Salas on RRL surveys, DAmato on Band 5a dual-AGN confirmation, and Emig on RRL spectral energy distributions. The multi-tier continuum surveys, arcsecond HI and deepest polarimetry remain tied to the full AA4 design baseline.

sections.section_summary:
The Cosmos section is organised around three connected science drivers: precision cosmology from large-scale structure, the physics of the high-redshift intergalactic medium during Cosmic Dawn and reionisation, and the non-thermal and magnetised content of galaxy clusters and the cosmic web. The cosmology chapters (Fonseca, Camera, Harrison, Wolz, Nasirudin, Bosi, Asorey) converge on a small set of reference surveys inherited from the Cosmology Red Book: a single-dish Wide Band 1 HI intensity-mapping survey of about 20,000 deg2 in roughly 10,000 h, a Medium-Deep Band 2 survey of about 5,000 deg2 serving both HI galaxy redshifts and radio weak lensing, and a Band 1 continuum survey of the southern sky that reaches a flux limit near 20 uJy. These surveys feed primordial non-Gaussianity, BAO and redshift-drift measurements, Nx2pt analyses and cross-correlations with gravitational-wave catalogues. A pulsar-timing strand (Cruz, Perna, Pasechnik, Jenkins, Ragavendra) requires roughly 200 millisecond pulsars timed at about 100 ns over 10-20 years. A fast-radio-burst strand (Caleb) uses fluence thresholds and survey fields of view to predict counts and baryon constraints.

The observing modes follow from these drivers. Deep HI intensity mapping is the most frequently invoked mode: single-dish scanning in Band 1 for BAO and cross-correlation work, and interferometric mapping (Mazumder, Elahi) for smaller-scale clustering at z of 1 to 3. The EoR and Cosmic Dawn chapters (Barkana, Acharya, Bag, Chakraborty, Cang, de Lera Acedo) set their integrations around 1000-1080 h on SKA-Low for power spectra, with longer integrations on selected fields for tomographic imaging. The cluster and magnetism chapters take a different approach. Pointed or tiered continuum observations of 1-50 h with SKA-Low and SKA-Mid (Cassano, Santra, Cuciti, Gitti, Arpan Pal, Aritra Basu) target radio halos, relics, mini-halos and fluctuation-dynamo filaments. Polarimetric RM grids use SKA-Low near 150 MHz (O'Sullivan) and SKA-Mid Band 2 (Loi, Vacca, Kurahara). Band 5 carries the tSZ imaging (Perrott) and the depolarisation-free measurements of cluster magnetic fields.

How AA* compares with AA4 depends on the science case. For surface-brightness and power-spectrum work the difference is modest. O'Sullivan finds only a small sensitivity loss at 5 arcsec, so an RM grid could begin with AA* and continue with AA4. Fonseca and Regis report that AA* gives constraints close to AA4 for primordial non-Gaussianity and for dark-matter searches in the SKA-Mid bands. Cunnington argues that single-dish intensity mapping is well suited to early AA* operations. Other cases depend on the full array. Harrison shows that radio weak lensing is unachievable with AA* at any depth, because its PSF cannot resolve enough galaxy shapes, while AA4 meets the required density of about 1 galaxy per arcmin2. Perrott finds that high-fidelity tSZ imaging needs the dense short baselines of AA4. Bag concludes that 21-cm tomographic imaging is superior with AA4, and Regis finds SKA-Low dark-matter limits about three times weaker with AA*. The section therefore treats AA* as the stage for statistical detections and early surveys, and AA4 as the stage for the high-resolution imaging these measurements need.

sections.section_summary:
The Extreme Universe section gathers the compact-object, transient and astroparticle science cases, and its demands fall into three technical families. The largest is pulsar work. Keane et al. set out the census strategy that underpins most of the other pulsar chapters: real-time searches with 500 (250) tied-array beams on SKA-Low and 1500 (1125) beams on SKA-Mid at AA4 (AA*), using 10-minute pointings and an inner-kilometre sub-array. Several chapters build on that population. JunXu uses it for rotation measures of the Galactic magnetic field, Tiburzi for dispersion and scintillation studies of the ionised medium, Bagchi and Abbate for pulsars in globular clusters and the Galactic Centre, and Shannon, Venkatraman Krishnan, Basu, Oswald and Levin for timing arrays, tests of gravity, glitches, magnetospheres and neutron-star evolution. The second family covers time-domain astronomy: fast radio bursts (Curtin), long-period transients (Qiu), radio stars (Driessen), supernovae (Chandra; An), tidal disruption events (An; Shu), gravitational-wave counterparts (Colombo; Capelo) and neutrino fields (Rösch). These cases depend on commensal or triggered observations and on the transient buffer, and they ask for SKA-Mid continuum depths of roughly 1 to 10 microJy per beam in 10 minutes to a few hours.

The third family is VLBI with a phased SKA-Mid. It is the most frequently cited technique in the section. In this mode the SKA becomes the most sensitive element of global arrays, reaching image noise of a few microJy per beam in about an hour with beams of 0.5 to 1 mas at 8 to 15 GHz. This capability drives the proposed programmes on gamma-ray bursts (Giarratana), colliding-wind binaries (Marcote), X-ray binaries (An; Lin), jets at high redshift (Spingola), blazars and novae (Kadler; Lico), and space VLBI (Kovalev). Band 5 recurs throughout the section. It reduces free-free absorption and scattering, which is why the Galactic Centre searches, the core-shift measurements and the studies of young supernova shocks all rely on it. For the same reason, Bignall, Abbate and Tiburzi each argue that Bands 3 and 4 are needed to close the 1.76 to 4.6 GHz gap. A small group of astroparticle chapters (Buitink, Corstanje, Watanabe, Nelles) uses the dense core of SKA-Low as a detector of air showers between 50 and 350 MHz.

The papers are candid about the difference between AA* and AA4, and the difference matters most where sensitivity compounds over time or where the core is thinned. The air-shower programmes state that AA* already holds about 90 per cent of the core antennas and is sufficient for their goals. Capelo, in a similar vein, finds that the number of radio counterparts to LISA sources barely changes between the two stages. In contrast, Keane shows that the SKA-Mid core is more hollowed out at AA* than the SKA-Low core, so pulsar survey speed suffers more on Mid. Venkatraman Krishnan concludes that binary-pulsar tests need AA4, which halves the uncertainties on post-Keplerian parameters and reaches a given precision one to two years sooner. Tiburzi, Basu and the VLBI chapters likewise treat AA4 as the stage that extends programmes demonstrated at AA* to fainter, more distant or quiescent sources and larger samples. Consequently, the section's programmes are designed to begin in AA* with the brightest targets and to reach their full scientific return only with AA4.

The formation and early evolution of relativistic jets from X-ray binaries remain among the most compelling puzzles in high-energy astrophysics (Mirabel and Rodríguez, 1994, 1999; Fender et al., 2004).

By comparing core shifts and inferred magnetic profiles across different accretion states and compact-object types, CoSMOS will test whether jet magnetization evolves systematically during outbursts and whether black-hole and neutron-star jets occupy the same parameter space.
An important puzzle presented to us is why pulsars are variable at all timescales imaginable.

LPTs have even longer periods (up to 6.45 hours discovered so far) (Lee et al., 2025) and it is as yet unclear whether these also originate from neutron stars, or from an alternative source or physical mechanism, such as from White Dwarfs (Rea et al., 2024).

While the notion that PWNe are primarily powered by the rotation energy of neutron stars was established nearly ∼ 6 decades ago (e.g., Pacini 1968; Goldreich and Julian 1969), as described below their remains several unanswered fundamental questions regarding the nature of these sources, especially concerning their ability to generate the highest energy photons - and therefore, among the highest energy particles - observed from the Milky Way.
While there is now ample evidence that this scenario is broadly correct, many details remain poorly understood.
Another long-standing open question is the nature of jet components and the transverse jet structure.
Whether the physical origin of the compact radio emission is due to weak outflow activity, advection dominated accretion flow, or star formation has long been debated.

sections.section_summary:
The Methods and Techniques section gathers the calibration, imaging, inference and array-extension work that other SKA science cases depend on, rather than a single astrophysical target. Its papers fall into five groups. Cosmic magnetism is the first, and there polarimetric inference turns rotation-measure grids and Faraday spectra into magnetic-field constraints: Vacca, Carcamo and Chan model the Galactic foreground, run Faraday tomography across the SKA-Low and SKA-Mid bands, and forward-model polarised skies from MHD simulations. The second group treats the 21-cm signal from Cosmic Dawn and the Epoch of Reionisation (EoR), where foreground and systematics control dominates (Burba, Acharya, Zhang). Calibration against the ionosphere is the third (Morgan, Datta). The fourth is time-domain operations, meaning commensal image-plane searches, rapid-response triggering and technosignature searches (Andersson, Anderson, Tremblay). A large VLBI cluster forms the fifth. It proposes extending both telescopes to intercontinental baselines for astrometry, geodesy, tests of general relativity and pulsar parallaxes (Chen, Bempong-Manful, Li, Kobayashi, Timmerman, Xu, Wongphechauxsorn, Takahashi). Around these groups sit data-science chapters on source finding, AI, citizen science and radio weak-lensing shear measurement.

The observing modes follow from these groups. VLBI and astrometry dominate numerically, and the stated demands are concrete. Li quotes a 15 μJy sensitivity at 15 GHz in 300 s over 0.256 GHz, which yields single-epoch astrometric precision of about 2 μas. Kobayashi estimates fringe-detection limits near 0.1–0.2 mJy on SKA-Low baselines at 320 MHz. Takahashi calls for about 30 one-hour epochs over 2–3 years to reach distances good to 1 pc for millisecond pulsars used in pulsar timing arrays. Polarimetry and RM-grid work rests on the Band 2 survey of 30,000 deg² at 2″ and 4 μJy that Vacca cites, and on the calculator estimates in Carcamo. The EoR chapters require calibration errors below about 10⁻⁵ and sky models complete to 1–10 mJy. The time-domain chapters depend less on raw sensitivity than on data products: fast snapshot imaging, transient buffers, zoom channels at 14 Hz and 210 Hz, and tied-array beams. The ionosphere chapters mainly need station-level imaging and access to visibilities.

Most chapters say their methods work from AA*, so the difference between AA* and AA4 is usually one of depth rather than feasibility. Andersson states that the commensal transient tools apply to all deployments from AA* onward, and Tremblay sizes the technosignature data products explicitly for AA*. Carcamo gives Band 2 sensitivities of 5.4 μJy/beam at AA* and 2.9 μJy/beam at AA4 for a 16-hour RM-grid pointing. Robishaw is where the gap between stages matters most. Zeeman detection in LMC masers takes 3 minutes with AA4 against 10 minutes with AA*, but a search for OH masers in M31 needs 36 hours with AA4 and an impractical 115 hours with AA*. Morgan, in contrast, expects the smaller AA* core to matter little for ionospheric science, while the extra outer stations of AA4 would help refractive-shift and parallax measurements. Several VLBI proposals go beyond both stages, because they need baselines of thousands of kilometres from new stations in Africa, Australia and Asia.

open_questions.quote: Despite magnetic fields been observed up to galaxy cluster scales and in filaments between clusters through synchrotron emission (e.g., Govoni et al. 2019, Vernstrom et al. 2023), firm constraints on magneto-genesis scenarios have been not placed yet.
Yet the origin, strength, and structure of these vast magnetic fields remain poorly constrained (Vazza et al., 2018; Brüggen et al., 2020).
However, the differences between primordial and astrophysical seeding are often subtle and can overlap, particularly in regions dominated by nonlinear evolution such as galaxy clusters.
This choice is motivated by the assumption that lower-amplitude modes would be noise-dominated, although the present test cases are noise-free.
However, at the SKAO AA* sensitivity predictions, the rate of variable and transient sources will likely be too great for such citizen science efforts to be employed on the entire SKAO datastream.

Moreover, the widely used assumption of foreground spectral smoothness can break down in the presence of polarized emission affected by Faraday rotation, introducing additional spectral complexity (Spinelli et al., 2019a; Sobey et al., 2018).

Note that there is a controversy over the interpretation of the retarded term (e.g., Will, 2003; Fomalont and Kopeikin, 2007; Will, 2014). SKA-VLBI may provide an opportunity to resolve this controversy.

Moreover, while the development of a robust methodology to account for the possibility that, in this frequency band, the calibrator is extended rather than point-like remains a topic for future work, such corrections should, in principle, be implementable provided that the calibrator exhibits no significant variability over the duration of the astrometry observations.
While the size of the MWA would provide good sensitivity, the long-term future of the MWAfacility, e.g. past cycle 0 or 1 of SKA-Low, is still being decided.
Given the relatively recent rise of artificial intelligence techniques in astronomy, it would be fair to say that it is as-yet unclear what the ultimate impact of ML on the SKA will be.

open_questions.quote: Furthermore, first results from the SKA Science Data Challenge 3b on inference (SDC3b 4 ), where the global ionization fraction at three different redshifts was to be blindly derived from 2DPS generated with two different simulators, point towards current posterior estimators to be susceptible to model misspecification both from signal and noise modelling; this has also been pointed out previously (Zhou and La Plante, 2022).
Although Busch (2024) has recently used the Green Bank Telescope (GBT) to detect thermal 18 cm OH emission in the Andromeda Galaxy, OH masers have yet to be detected in M31.
Cronyn (1972) provide a theoretical framework for working instead with interferometric visibilities, which, to our knowledge has never been tested.

The only tentative association between a BNS merger and FRB was reported for GW190425 and CHIME FRB 20190425A by Moroianu et al. (2023), however, further modelling suggests this is a chance coincidence (Bhardwaj et al., 2024).

Although there has been a great deal of growth in this field, the greatest challenge remains to expand the sensitivity, sky coverage, emission modalities, and signal detection and filtering algorithms to set more stringent limits on the prevalence of technological life in the Universe.
Nevertheless, a more comprehensive characterization of the finite inner and outer scales at the Murchison Radio-astronomy Observatory (MRO) remains necessary.
